questions.q: Why does Kubernetes send SIGTERM before SIGKILL when terminating a pod's container?
options: To give the process a chance to finish in-flight work and shut down gracefully before being forcibly killed
Because SIGTERM restarts the container automatically
SIGTERM and SIGKILL do the same thing
questions.explain: SIGTERM is catchable and lets a process clean up and finish in-flight work; SIGKILL is immediate and uncatchable, used only after the grace period expires.

questions.q: What does systemd provide that a plain init script does not?
options: Parallelized, dependency-aware startup, automatic restart policies, and structured logging via journald
questions.explain: systemd manages service dependencies and startup order, offers restart policies like Restart=on-failure, and logs through journald, none of which a basic sequential init script provides.

questions.q: In the Linux DNS resolution order, what is typically checked before querying a DNS server?
options: Nothing is checked before querying a DNS server
questions.explain: The resolver checks /etc/hosts for a static entry, then consults /etc/nsswitch.conf to determine lookup order, before falling back to the resolvers in /etc/resolv.conf.

questions.q: What are the three steps of the TCP three-way handshake, in order?
questions.explain: The client sends SYN, the server responds SYN-ACK, and the client replies ACK — only then does the connection become ESTABLISHED.

questions.q: Why does the NGINX Ingress in front of checkout use an HTTP-level readiness probe instead of just a TCP connection check?
options: TCP checks are slower than HTTP checks
HTTP checks are required by Kubernetes for all services
There is no difference between the two
A TCP check only confirms the port is open, not that the application itself is healthy
questions.explain: A bare TCP connect only proves the port accepts connections; an HTTP readiness probe actually verifies the application can process requests before routing traffic to it.
